entities.name: Abu Al-Hassan Al-Marini Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Abu al-Hassan Mosque (Mosque of Abu al-Hassan) in Salé, Morocco, built c. 1341 CE by Abu al-Hassan Ali ibn Othman — the Black Sultan, Marinid sultan of Morocco (r. 1331-1351) — is one of the finest examples of Marinid Islamic architecture in Morocco, a dynasty that produced some of the most exquisite medieval Islamic monuments including the Bou Inania Madrasa in Fez (1355 CE). Abu al-Hassan was the most powerful Marinid sultan, extending his rule briefly over all of the Maghreb and al-Andalus.

Abu al-Hassan (the Black Sultan, so called because his mother was a Sub-Saharan African slave) was renowned as both a military conqueror and a great patron of Islamic art and architecture. Under his reign, Moroccan-Andalusian artistic production reached its peak: the intricate stucco, zellij (geometric tilework), and carved cedarwood that characterize Marinid architecture were brought to their highest technical refinement. His mosque in Salé exemplifies this tradition.

Salé — across the Bou Regreg River from Rabat — was one of medieval Morocco's most important cities, and the Abu al-Hassan mosque is one of its most significant Islamic monuments. The mosque's mihrab, minaret, and decorative program demonstrate the sophisticated synthesis of Moroccan, Andalusian, and Eastern Islamic artistic traditions that characterize Marinid art at its peak. Abu al-Hassan's reign, though ultimately ended by defeat at the Battle of Taghaza (1347) and the Black Death, represents the Marinid dynasty's golden age.
